userMessage:
Transcript:
System Audio: Can you walk me through a time When you audited or optimized a CRM or ticketing

Retrieved memory to use if relevant:
1. Question: Can you walk me through a time when you audited and or optimized a CRM or ticketing system to improve frontline agent efficiency?
Sample answer: In my previous role, I audited our Zendesk instance and discovered that agents were spending 30% of their time manually tagging tickets and routing them to the correct queues. I implemented a new automated routing logic using triggers and macros integrated with our CRM data. By streamlining the ticket intake process and automating categorization, I reduced average handle time by 15% and increased agent capacity, allowing the team to handle a 20% increase in ticket volume without additional headcount. (Source: Question bank - Apollo)
2. System Audio: I have some questions I will go through. They're mostly tell me about a time when type questions. I'm looking for specific examples so I can get an understanding of what exactly you did versus the team and what the impact was. Can you walk me through a time when you audited and or optimized a CRM or ticketing system to improve frontline agent efficiency?
System Audio: Have you had experience integrating GenAI or other automation controls directly into customer support workflows?
You: Yeah.
System Audio: Can you tell me about a time you had to align stakeholders across product, engineering, and operations on a technical project where the priorities conflicted? And how did you navigate that?
You: Yeah.
System Audio: How do you evaluate whether a change, tool, or workflow will have downstream effects on other systems or teams? Walk me through your process.
You: Yeah.
System Audio: Can you describe a time you designed or maintained an API-based integration between a customer experience platform and another internal system? If you have another example or can go deeper into that one, please do. (Source: 2026-05-27 Live Session.txt)
3. Question: Tell me about a time you identified a high-friction customer path and what you did to improve it.
Sample answer: I noticed that our onboarding support tickets were spiking due to a specific configuration step that users found confusing. By analyzing the interaction data, I identified the exact point of friction. I worked with the Product team to redesign the in-app guidance and simultaneously updated our automated support flows to provide proactive, context-aware help at that specific step. This reduced ticket volume for that issue by 25% and improved the overall onboarding completion rate. (Source: Question bank - Apollo)
4. Question: How have you improved queue management and team efficiency at Sigma?
Sample answer: I implemented reusable workflows in Intercom to automate ticket snoozing and follow-ups, which prevented backlogs. I also gamified ticket handling during peak times by creating a 'coin' system for agents who grabbed tickets from the queue, which increased motivation and responsiveness. (Source: Question bank - Apollo)

cards.question: And then have you had any integrating Gen AI or other automation tools directly into customer support?

userMessage:
Transcript:
System Audio: Can you tell me about a time you had to Line stakeholders across product engineering

Retrieved memory to use if relevant:
1. Question: Can you tell me about a time you had to align stakeholders across product, engineering, and operations on a technical project where the priorities conflicted? And how did you navigate that?
Sample answer: I once led a project to integrate our support platform with our product database to provide agents with real-time user data. Engineering was concerned about API load, while Product wanted to prioritize new feature development. I navigated this by presenting a data-backed business case showing that the integration would reduce ticket resolution time by 40%, which directly impacted customer retention. I proposed a phased rollout to mitigate engineering's performance concerns and established a cross-functional steering committee to ensure alignment throughout the project lifecycle. (Source: Question bank - Apollo)
2. Question: Tell me about a time you pushed back on a stakeholder or leader because you believed they were heading in the wrong direction. How did you handle it? And what was the outcome.
Sample answer: A VP of Tech Support proposed migrating our entire Zendesk workflow to a proprietary internal platform to save costs. I analyzed the scope and realized the migration effort would far outweigh any potential efficiency gains. I collaborated with a senior team member to gather data on the complexity of the move and presented a business case to the VP, recommending we pause the migration for several quarters to focus on higher-impact initiatives. The leadership team agreed, and we avoided a costly, low-value project. (Source: Question bank - Apollo)
3. System Audio: I have some questions I will go through. They're mostly tell me about a time when type questions. I'm looking for specific examples so I can get an understanding of what exactly you did versus the team and what the impact was. Can you walk me through a time when you audited and or optimized a CRM or ticketing system to improve frontline agent efficiency?
System Audio: Have you had experience integrating GenAI or other automation controls directly into customer support workflows?
You: Yeah.
System Audio: Can you tell me about a time you had to align stakeholders across product, engineering, and operations on a technical project where the priorities conflicted? And how did you navigate that?
You: Yeah.

parsedCards.title: Answer
parsedCards.question: Can you tell me about a time you had to align stakeholders across product, engineering, and operations on a technical project where the priorities conflicted? And how did you navigate that?
bullets: I led support automation and systems integration work at Benchmark across Freshdesk, Zendesk, and RingCentral, and I aligned Product, Engineering, and Support Operations by framing decisions around agent efficiency and customer impact, not just tooling preferences.

When priorities conflicted, I brought data to the table—specifically the improvements we were targeting in first response time, average handle time, and resolution time—and used that to negotiate a phased rollout that reduced risk while still delivering early wins.

I kept alignment tight by setting clear ownership and feedback loops, then translating support insights into product and service improvements so each group could see how their constraints were respected and how the changes improved frontline execution.

cards.question: Can you tell me about a time you had to align stakeholders across product, engineering, and operations on a technical project where the priorities conflicted? And how did you navigate that?
bullets: I owned executive escalation management for SEV 0 and SEV 1 incidents, and I aligned Engineering, Product, Customer Success, and stakeholders on triage, communication, and post-incident follow-up to keep decisions and messaging consistent.

Retrieved memory to use if relevant:
1. Question: How do you evaluate whether a change, tool, or workflow will have downstream effects on other systems or teams? Walk me through your process.
Sample answer: My process begins with a comprehensive impact analysis. First, I map out the data flow between the affected system and all integrated platforms, such as Salesforce or our internal data warehouse. I then conduct stakeholder interviews with leads from affected teams to identify potential friction points. Finally, I perform a 'dry run' in a sandbox environment to test the integration and monitor for unexpected behavior. I document all dependencies and create a rollback plan before any production deployment to ensure business continuity. (Source: Question bank - Apollo)
2. System Audio: I have some questions I will go through. They're mostly tell me about a time when type questions. I'm looking for specific examples so I can get an understanding of what exactly you did versus the team and what the impact was. Can you walk me through a time when you audited and or optimized a CRM or ticketing system to improve frontline agent efficiency?
System Audio: Have you had experience integrating GenAI or other automation controls directly into customer support workflows?
You: Yeah.
System Audio: Can you tell me about a time you had to align stakeholders across product, engineering, and operations on a technical project where the priorities conflicted? And how did you navigate that?
You: Yeah.
System Audio: How do you evaluate whether a change, tool, or workflow will have downstream effects on other systems or teams? Walk me through your process.
You: Yeah.
System Audio: Can you describe a time you designed or maintained an API-based integration between a customer experience platform and another internal system? If you have another example or can go deeper into that one, please do. (Source: 2026-05-27 Live Session.txt)

4. certain cases where it makes sense—and not automating everything just to automate it—took a little effort. Everyone is in the mode right now where they want to automate everything, and that is great. The more you automate the better, but sometimes not automating it fully is even better. It depends on what it is and if human touch or human empathy plays a role. We are walking that line and trying to figure out what we should be automating as much as we can and what we shouldn't.
Candidate (Stephen): It affects other teams as well, so it took a lot of one-off meetings with other team leads to sit down and figure out what processes that affect both of us or current workflows we want to revamp versus leave alone. That has been a challenge just because the workflows affect so many different teams. Getting them in a room and talking about what we want in the future was a challenge, but it is going.
